/-!
# Erdős Problem 214

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/214](https://www.erdosproblems.com/214)
- [CsTo94] Csizmadia, György and Tóth, Géza, *Note on a Ramsey-type problem in geometry*.
  J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1994), 302-306.
- [EGMRSS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Montgomery, P. and Rothschild, B. L. and Spencer, J.
  and Straus, E. G., *Euclidean Ramsey theorems. II*. (1975), 529-557.
- [Ju79] Juhász, Rozália, *Ramsey type theorems in the plane*. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (1979),
  152-160.
-/

open scoped Congruent EuclideanGeometry

namespace Erdos214

/-- The four vertices of a unit square. -/
def unitSquare : Fin 4 → ℝ² := ![!₂[0, 0], !₂[1, 0], !₂[1, 1], !₂[0, 1]]

/-- Colouring the points of `S` blue and the points of `Sᶜ` red gives a red/blue colouring of
$\mathbb{R}^2$; it is unit-distance-avoiding if no two blue points are distance $1$ apart. -/
def UnitDistanceAvoiding (S : Set ℝ²) : Prop := ∀ x ∈ S, ∀ y ∈ S, dist x y ≠ 1

/-- Any unit-distance-avoiding colouring contains a congruent red copy of every set of `n`
points. -/
def HasRedCopies (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ S : Set ℝ², UnitDistanceAvoiding S → ∀ K : Fin n → ℝ², Function.Injective K →
    ∃ p : Fin n → ℝ², (∀ i, p i ∈ Sᶜ) ∧ (p ≅ K)

/-- The largest integer `k` such that any unit-distance-avoiding colouring contains a congruent
red copy of every set of `k` points. -/
noncomputable def k : ℕ := sSup {n | HasRedCopies n}

/--
Let $S\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be such that no two points in $S$ are distance $1$ apart. Must the
complement of $S$ contain four points which form a unit square?

The answer is yes, proved by Juhász [Ju79], who proved more generally that the complement of $S$
must contain a congruent copy of any set of four points.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos214.lean"]
theorem erdos_214 : answer(True) ↔
    ∀ S : Set ℝ², UnitDistanceAvoiding S →
      ∃ p : Fin 4 → ℝ², (∀ i, p i ∈ Sᶜ) ∧ (p ≅ unitSquare) := by
  sorry

/--
The answer is yes, proved by Juhász [Ju79], who proved more generally that the complement of $S$
must contain a congruent copy of any set of four points.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_214.variants.juhasz : HasRedCopies 4 := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus [EGMRSS75] had earlier showed that
$3\leq k\leq 10^{12}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_214.variants.egmrss : 3 ≤ k ∧ k ≤ 10 ^ 12 := by
  sorry

/--
Juhász [Ju79] also improved the upper bound to $k\leq 11$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_214.variants.juhasz_twelve_points : ¬ HasRedCopies 12 := by
  sorry

/--
The upper bound was improved further by Csizmadia and Tóth [CsTo94] to $k\leq 7$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_214.variants.csizmadia_toth : ¬ HasRedCopies 8 := by
  sorry

/--
The best known bounds currently are
$$4\leq k\leq 7.$$
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_214.variants.bounds : 4 ≤ k ∧ k ≤ 7 := by
  sorry

end Erdos214

reformulations.difference: Uses injective Fin n-indexed configurations and pairwise-distance congruence rather than finite point sets and rigid motions. The copied configuration p is not explicitly required to be injective.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every n-point set admits an injective Fin n enumeration. Congruence to an injective K forces p to be injective, since coincident p-values imply zero distance between the corresponding K-values. In Euclidean space, equal pairwise distances also give an ambient rigid motion: after choosing an anchor, the difference vectors have identical Gram matrices, inducing an isometry of their spans that extends to an orthogonal map of the plane; translation restores the anchor. The empty configuration causes no difficulty. The injectivity equivalence was proved in scratch, but the full rigid-motion characterization was not formalized.

reformulations.difference: Defines the largest admissible size using a natural-number sSup.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The admissible sizes are nonempty (HasRedCopies 0 holds) and downward closed: extend a smaller configuration by fresh points, apply the larger-size property, and restrict its red copy. The published eight-point counterexample therefore bounds all admissible sizes by 7. A nonempty bounded subset of ℕ contains its supremum, so this sSup is exactly the source's largest integer; the unbounded-set default value 0 is unreachable here. Scratch proves downward closure and k = m ↔ IsGreatest {n | HasRedCopies n} m with the published boundedness fact kept as an explicit premise.

reformulations.difference: States ¬ HasRedCopies 12 instead of the source's upper bound k ≤ 11.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Classical negation expands this into a unit-distance-avoiding S and an injective twelve-point configuration K such that every congruent copy meets S: precisely a twelve-point counterexample. Downward closure makes failure at 12 imply failure at every larger size. Since k is the maximum admissible size, this is equivalent to k ≤ 11. Scratch proves the counterexample characterization without additional hypotheses and the upper-bound equivalence with boundedness explicit.

reformulations.difference: States ¬ HasRedCopies 8 rather than explicitly giving the coloring/configuration counterexample or stating k ≤ 7.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Negating HasRedCopies 8 gives an avoiding set S and an injective eight-point K for which every congruent copy contains a point of S. After exchanging the paper's color names, this is exactly Csizmadia–Tóth's Theorem 1. Downward closure and the maximum characterization of k make it equivalent to k ≤ 7. Both the counterexample characterization and the boundedness-conditional upper-bound equivalence were checked in Lean.

review.notes: Checked all four definitions and six theorem statements. The source records the affirmative answer, Lean verification, and the same bounds as the file. Scratch tests in /workspace/review/scratch.lean verify the square's vertices and distances, inherited injectivity, empty/singleton cases, satisfiability of the hypotheses, supremum boundary behavior, and the stated reformulations, without depending on the problem's sorry theorems. Juhász's original full text was inaccessible; its four- and twelve-point results are corroborated by the Erdős page and Csizmadia–Tóth's introduction. The linked four-point proof, which implies the main square statement, replayed with only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound after four scratch-only tactic-compatibility edits for the sandbox's Lean 4.33.1 (the linked file targets 4.29.1). The reviewed file was not modified.
